Qibya

Massacre · 1953-10-14 · Jordanian-controlled West Bank

1953-10-14

Summary

The Qibya massacre occurred during heightened tensions along the Jordan-Israel armistice line. Following the October 12, 1953 killing of an Israeli woman and her two children in Yehud, Israel launched 'Operation Shoshana'—a large-scale reprisal attack on the Jordanian village of Qibya.

Unit 101, led by 25-year-old Major Ariel Sharon, attacked with approximately half a battalion of soldiers. After a mortar barrage, demolition squads systematically destroyed homes with inhabitants inside using explosives and grenades. Sharon later wrote the operation was meant to be 'an example for everyone' with orders for 'maximal killing and damage to property.'

The UN Mixed Armistice Commission condemned the attack as a breach of the Israel-Jordan armistice agreement. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 101 expressing 'strongest censure.' The US State Department called it 'shocking' and suspended economic aid to Israel. Despite international condemnation, no perpetrators were prosecuted.

Testimony

Ariel Sharon
“Sharon wrote in his memoir that he received orders: 'Qibya was to be an example for everyone.' He described ordering 'maximal killing and damage to property.' In autobiography 'Warrior': 'The orders were utterly clear.'”
Sharon, Ariel. 'Warrior: An Autobiography' (1989)
David Ben-Gurion
“Initially claimed attack was carried out by Israeli civilians acting on their own: 'border settlers in Israel...who were tired of the bloodshed.' Later privately acknowledged military operation. Stated: 'It doesn't make any real difference what will be said about Qibya around the world.'”
Knesset speech, October 1953; Sharett Diary
Major General Vagn Bennike
“Reported to UN Security Council that attack conducted by 'roughly half a battalion strength of soldiers from Israeli regular army' using mortars, Bangalore torpedoes, and TNT explosives in coordinated military operation.”
Report to UN Security Council, October 1953
Moshe Sharett
“In private diary opposed the operation: 'I told Lavon that this will be a grave error...it was never proved that reprisal actions serve their declared purpose.' Later wrote: 'I must underline that when I opposed the action I didn't even remotely suspect such a bloodbath.'”
Moshe Sharett Diary, October 14, 1953
Jordanian Foreign Minister
“Reported to UN: 'massacre of sixty-six inhabitants by organized military forces of Israel.' Called emergency MAC meeting. Described systematic demolition of homes and civilian casualties as unprecedented attack.”
Statement to UN Security Council, November 1953

War crimes

House-to-House Killings
Soldiers systematically threw grenades through doors and windows, then demolished houses with explosives while civilians remained inside. Bodies found buried in rubble.
UN MAC Report
Women and Children Targeted
Of 69 killed, two-thirds were women and children. Families trapped in homes as explosives detonated.
US State Dept
Deliberate Civilian Infrastructure Destruction
School and mosque systematically demolished. 45 houses destroyed with explosives—approximately 22% of village housing stock.
Systematic Looting
Shops looted during operation. Unused explosives found dropped by attackers, indicating extensive demolition supplies brought to scene.
US Archives
Prevention of Rescue
Israeli forces shelled neighboring villages Budrus (43 mortar shells) and Shuqba to prevent Jordanian Arab Legion from reaching Qibya to assist civilians.
US State Dept Cable

Legal classification

Armistice Agreement Violations (1949)
Article II & III breaches: Unprovoked military attack across armistice line into Jordanian territory. Mixed Armistice Commission found Israel in 'clear breach' of agreement.
Customary International Humanitarian Law
Distinction principle: Failed to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Deliberate targeting of civilian homes, school, and mosque.
Modern Classification (Descriptive)
Under contemporary international law (Geneva Conventions, Rome Statute), actions would constitute: willful killing of civilians, extensive destruction not justified by military necessity, attacks on civilian objects.
Armistice Agreement Violations (1949)
Disproportionate force: Response to one incident (3 deaths) with military operation killing 69 civilians deemed grossly disproportionate by international observers.
Customary International Humanitarian Law
Proportionality: UN and international community condemned attack as massively disproportionate retaliation.
Modern Classification (Descriptive)
UN Security Council Resolution 101 described attack as 'inconsistent with obligations under the Charter.'
Customary International Humanitarian Law
Unnecessary suffering: Use of explosives on occupied civilian homes caused preventable death and suffering.

Commanders

1928-2014 Ariel Sharon
Commanded Unit 101 during Qibya operation. Led approximately 600 troops in attack. Later wrote orders were for 'maximal killing and damage.' Never prosecuted. Subsequently served as Defense Minister (1981-83) and Prime Minister (2001-2006).
1915-1981 Moshe Dayan
Supervised planning of Operation Shoshana. Approved Sharon's operational plan for Qibya attack. Chief of Staff during 1956 Suez Crisis operations. Later Defense Minister (1967, 1969-74). Never faced accountability for 1953 operation.
1886-1973 David Ben-Gurion
Authorized Operation Shoshana and reprisal policy. After massacre, falsely claimed attack carried out by Israeli civilians, not military. Later privately acknowledged military responsibility. Stated: 'It doesn't make any real difference what will be said about Qibya around the world.'
1904-1976 Pinhas Lavon
Temporary Defense Minister while Ben-Gurion on leave. Approved Operation Shoshana. Foreign Minister Moshe Sharett opposed operation but Lavon proceeded with approval of Ben-Gurion.
